title: Misinformation in the media: global coverage of GMOs 2019-2021
screen_reason: Content analysis of 535 English-language mainstream/online news articles on GMOs (12 January 2019 - 12 January 2021), each manually rated factual or containing misinformation against stated scientific consensus. Reports a verbatim share of items classified as misinformation (47/535 = 9 %) and the same share weighted by potential readership (256 million of 5 billion = 5 %). Item-level falsity against an external ground truth with a stated denominator = CONTENT; the readership-weighted figure has a consumption-style denominator and is coded EXPOSURE with borderline=true because the readership is Cision 'gross reach' (potential, modelled) rather than observed views. Regional shares (Africa about 20 %, North America 5 %, Europe 7 %) are reported but not rowed - see missed_or_uncertain for the reasons.

estimates.country: Top worldwide English-language online news media, plus an added selection of top outlets from anglophone sub-Saharan African countries
estimates.platform: Mainstream and online news media (Cision Media NextGen database)
estimates.measure_type: % of GMO news articles rated as containing misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 47 of 535 articles rated as containing misinformation (9 %); 488 rated factual (91 %) [Table 1]
estimates.denominator: 535 English-language news and online articles about GMOs retrieved with a GMO Boolean string (three or more GMO keywords) from a predetermined list of top English-language outlets plus added anglophone sub-Saharan African outlets
estimates.definition: article manually rated as containing content at variance with generally-accepted scientific facts on GMOs (e.g. unqualified or unrebutted claims that GM crops/foods harm health)
estimates.misinfo_def: We use the term "misinformation" in a broad definition to include both "mis" and "dis" information (the latter is usually termed to include intentional falsehood, while the former may be unintentional), and use the term "misinformation" to label content in news media that is at variance with generally-accepted scientific facts on the GMO issue
estimates.source_quote: Table 1. Occurrence of GMO misinformation, January 2019 – January 2021. Factual Misinformation Total Articles number 488 47 535 Percentage 91% 9% 100%
estimates.page_loc: Results, pp. 20-21; Table 1 'Occurrence of GMO misinformation, January 2019 - January 2021'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Articles manually rated by the authors (The Alliance for Science; Cision Global Insights) as factual or containing misinformation, benchmarked to stated scientific-consensus positions (US National Academies of Sciences, AAAS board, WHO, UK Royal Society). Number of coders, coder training and inter-rater reliability are not reported; the full ratings are in a supplementary spreadsheet. Declared interests: the Alliance for Science is a pro-biotechnology organisation funded in part by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, and Cision performs media analysis for paying clients including that foundation.
estimates.moderator_quote: To build up a database of articles, we searched the Cision Media NextGen platform to identify every article from a pre-determined list (see Supplementary Information for the full list) of top English-language media that contained three or more GMO-related keywords. ... We added a selection of top news media from anglophone sub-Saharan African countries to more closely evaluate GMO misinformation in this region.
estimates.notes: This is the paper's headline figure ('an overall falsehood rate of 9%' in the abstract) and the only whole-corpus item-level share. Data collection spans 12 Jan 2019 - 12 Jan 2021, so year is coded as the start year 2019 (midpoint 2020); publication year 2022 (journal issue dated 2025). The outlet frame is a curated list of 'top' English-language media with a deliberate African over-weight, so denom_selection=curated and the corpus is not a random or census sample of world media.

estimates.moderator_quote: We define readership as the total potential reach of a media item, whether print or online. For a full description for how readership is calculated for this approach, see "gross reach" in Evanega. et al., 2022.13
estimates.notes: BORDERLINE / JUDGEMENT CALL: the denominator is potential readership (views), which by the denominator rule points to EXPOSURE, but 'potential reach' is a modelled audience upper bound attached to outlets, not observed consumption by identified people. An adjudicator could defensibly recode this as an audience-weighted CONTENT share instead of EXPOSURE. It is the same 535-article corpus as the 9 % row, weighted differently, so the two rows must not be pooled as independent estimates.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) REGIONAL SHARES REPORTED BUT NOT ROWED: the paper states 'About 20% - a fifth - of Africa's GMO media content in our database is rated as misinformation. The corresponding proportion is 5% for North America and 7% for Europe.' (Results p. 23, accompanying Figure 5; the Africa figure is also an abstract headline - 'About a fifth of Africa's media coverage on GMOs contained misinformation' - and the conclusion repeats 'misinformation rates as high as a 20%'). I did not create rows for the three regions because (a) no regional denominators are given anywhere in the text - the article counts by region exist only inside Figure 5, which the text rendering does not reproduce; (b) they are subsets of the SAME 535-article corpus as the 9 % row, so they cannot enter a pooled analysis alongside it as independent estimates; and (c) the authors state the regional comparison is not valid, 'we cannot make a true comparison to other regions as we intentionally highlighted African media for special investigation in our media list, thus biasing it for this purpose'. A practical constraint reinforces this: the PDF's two-column layout is interleaved line by line in the text rendering, so no contiguous verbatim span carries the regional sentence. VALUES FOR THE RECORD, for an adjudicator who wants these rows from the published PDF (p. 23): Africa 20 %, North America 5 %, Europe 7 %, all with country_scope=multi and the same instrument and moderator coding as the global CONTENT row. (2) TOPIC BREAKDOWNS NOT ROWED: topic-level shares of the same corpus - human health 28 of 247 articles = 11 %, pesticides 16 of 150 = 11 %, and readership-based within-topic shares (animal health 13 % of readership on 1 of 21 articles, human health 7 %, pesticides 6 %, environment 6 %). These are subgroups of one corpus and the topic categories overlap by design ('the total number of GMO topic mentions in volume terms (821) is greater than our total number of articles (535) because some articles reference more than one topic'), so they cannot be pooled; per R4 the whole-corpus figure was kept. (3) COMPOSITION OF THE MISINFORMATION SET NOT ROWED: 40 % of the 'misinformation conversation' by volume was human health and 25 % environment; by readership 35 % human health, 26 % pesticides, 21 % environment. These are shares WITHIN the misinformation-only set and describe composition, not prevalence. (4) SENTIMENT: 100 % of misinformation articles were rated negative, mixed or neutral and none positive - a property of the misinformation set, not a prevalence share. (5) Figures 1-5 are not in the text extraction (captions only), so regional and topic denominators are unavailable. (6) COMPARISON FIGURES CITED FROM THE AUTHORS' OWN EARLIER WORK (about 0.1 % primary misinformation in COVID-19 vaccine news; 2.9 % of COVID-19 pandemic coverage) belong to other papers and are barred by R8. (7) Year coded 2019 for a 12 Jan 2019 - 12 Jan 2021 collection window.

rob.design: Retrospective media content analysis. Frame: every article containing three or more GMO-related keywords, in a predetermined list of top English-language outlets (list in Supplementary Information) plus a deliberately added set of top anglophone sub-Saharan African outlets, retrieved from the Cision Media NextGen platform for 12 January 2019 - 12 January 2021; a Boolean string iteratively refined; 535 relevant articles. Coding: articles manually assigned to one or more of six topic categories (821 topic mentions for 535 articles), manually coded for sentiment (positive/negative/neutral/mixed), and manually rated factual vs containing misinformation against stated scientific-consensus positions. Not reported: number of coders, coder qualifications, training, blinding, or any inter-rater reliability statistic; no sampling probability; regional comparability explicitly compromised by the deliberate African over-weight. Readership is Cision 'gross reach' (potential audience), not measured views. Declared interests: authors from the Alliance for Science (pro-biotechnology, part-funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation) and Cision Global Insights (commercial media analysis for paying clients including that foundation).
rob.item6_quote: We use the term "misinformation" in a broad definition to include both "mis" and "dis" information (the latter is usually termed to include intentional falsehood, while the former may be unintentional), and use the term "misinformation" to label content in news media that is at variance with generally-accepted scientific facts on the GMO issue, as discussed above.
rob.item10_quote: We found a total of 535 relevant articles for the 2-year period in which we searched our media database with the GMO Boolean search string. Of these, we rated 488 as factual and 47 as containing misinformation ... Overall, about 9% of the articles published on GMOs from 2019–2021 that we reviewed contained misinformation, while 91% were factually accurate.
